title: Gold doubles in a year as inflation passes 12 percent
what: Gold averaged 455 dollars an ounce in December, 16 percent more than in November and more than twice its price of a year ago. Consumer prices in November were 12.6 percent higher than a year earlier. Since the Federal Reserve under its new chairman Paul Volcker said on 6 October that it would control the supply of money rather than steer interest rates, the rate banks charge each other has run near 14 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 13.8 percent. Inflation 12.6 percent. Unemployment 5.9 percent.
why: The opening position of the game: double-digit inflation, a Fed that has just changed course, and gold in a speculative run that peaks a month later. Every rates story of the next forty years starts from here.
source: data/out/gold.json (LBMA monthly averages via datahub.io/core/gold-prices, read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCNS (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/anti-inflation-measures (read 2026-10-03)

title: Gold hits a record above 840 dollars
what: On 21 January the London gold fixing reached a record 843 dollars an ounce, three days after silver touched 49.45 dollars. Gold averaged 675 dollars in January, almost half as much again as in December. Buyers want metal instead of money after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, with American hostages still held in Tehran and consumer prices 13.3 percent higher in December than a year earlier.
why: The top of gold's 1970s bull market. The January 1980 monthly average was not seen again until May 2006, and in real terms not for decades: the game's starkest lesson about buying at the peak of a panic.

title: The Fed's rate tumbles from 17.6 to 9.5 percent; bonds and gold bounce back
what: Interest rates are falling as fast as they rose. The Fed's interest rate, the rate at which banks lend to each other, averaged under 9.5 percent in June against 17.6 percent in April, because the economy is in recession. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable, because they still promise the old, higher return: the US Treasury 2000 has gained 19 percent since the end of March. It is still 23 percent below where it started the year, after the collapse of the first quarter. Gold rebounded and averaged 601 dollars, 17 percent more than in May. The numbers: the Fed's rate 9.5 percent. Inflation 14.4 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: Volcker's first squeeze ends in retreat: the Fed lets rates drop with the recession, and gold and long bond yields start rising again over the summer. Inflation was not yet beaten, which is why the second squeeze in the autumn had to be harder. The Treasury 2000 is down 23% since December 1979 (13.09 to 10.11), so the year-to-date figure the curator asked for is negative; the beat gives it together with the rebound since March. [Curator note applied 2026-10-04: "You should make a connection to how falling rates sends the price of bonds upwards. The article should mention the 2000 vintage bond price return ytd from the game."]
source: https://www.fedprimerate.com/wall_street_journal_prime_rate_history.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/INTDSRUSM193N (read 2026-10-03); data/out/gold.json (read 2026-10-03); bond price changes from data/out/ust2000.json

title: The Fed drives its interest rate to 19 percent
what: The Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker fights inflation by making money expensive. Its interest rate, the rate at which banks lend to each other, averaged nearly 19 percent in December; in July it was 9.0 percent. Banks pass this on to their customers: even the best ones now pay 21.5 percent for a loan. Gold averaged 538 dollars, 14 percent less than in November. The numbers: the Fed's rate 18.9 percent. Inflation 12.6 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: The defining number of the Volcker era. Money in a savings account now beats gold and shares on interest alone, and gold's twenty-year bear market has effectively begun.

title: The Fed holds its rate at 19 percent and gold slides below 410
what: The Federal Reserve has held its interest rate near 19 percent since May, as high as it has ever been. Consumer prices in June were 9.6 percent higher than a year earlier, so lenders now earn far more than inflation takes away, and saving pays better than owning gold. Gold averaged 409 dollars in July, 11 percent below June and the lowest since November 1979. The numbers: the Fed's rate 19.0 percent. Inflation 9.7 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: This is what 'real rates' mean in practice: a 10-point gap between interest and inflation. Gold has lost almost 40 percent from its January 1980 average and keeps falling.

title: The Fed's rate eases to 16 percent, but lending for ten years costs more than ever
what: The Fed's interest rate fell to just under 16 percent in September, from 19 percent in the summer. But investors who lend their money for ten years still demand more than ever before: the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds averaged 15.3 percent, against about 11.5 percent a year ago, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 18.4 percent. The S&P 500 lost 5 percent in the month as the economy weakens. Shares of companies whose profits lie far in the future, or that depend on borrowing, fell hardest: Apple Computer lost 24 percent, Sony 15, Schlumberger 14 and Intel 13, while steady earners such as McDonald's and Coca-Cola rose. The numbers: the Fed's rate 15.9 percent. Inflation 10.8 percent. Unemployment 7.4 percent.
why: The all-time high in long-term US interest rates and the low point for bond prices. Anyone who locked in these yields made the trade of a lifetime: the great bond bull market starts from here, though nobody could know it this month. [Curator note applied 2026-10-04: "Add comment about Apple, Sony, Schlumberger and others declining"]
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GS10 (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/recession-of-1981-82 (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MORTGAGE30US (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCNS (read 2026-10-03); data/out/ust2000.json (read 2026-10-03); price changes from data/out; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, CPIAUCSL and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)

title: Gold falls to 330 dollars as inflation retreats
what: Gold averaged 330 dollars in March, 12 percent below February, the lowest since August 1979 and less than half its January 1980 average. Inflation has dropped to 7.6 percent (February) while the rate banks charge each other is near 15 percent, so money in the bank earns about 7 percent more than prices rise. The prime rate stands at 16.5 percent.
why: Gold's first bottom of the Volcker years. Falling inflation plus very high interest rates is the worst combination for a metal that pays nothing.

title: Gold jumps 20 percent as rates fall and Mexico wobbles
what: Gold averaged 437 dollars in September, 20 percent more than in August and almost 40 percent above its June average. Falling interest rates make gold cheaper to hold, and Mexico's announcement in August that it cannot pay its foreign debts has raised fears for the banks that lent to it. Ten-year Treasury yields averaged 12.3 percent, down from 14.3 percent in June.
why: A sharp counter-rally inside gold's long decline, driven by the same rate cuts that lit the stock market. It fades within months.

title: Gold slumps after OPEC cuts the oil price
what: Gold averaged 420 dollars in March, 14 percent below February's 491. On 14 March OPEC cut its base oil price from 34 to 29 dollars a barrel, the first cut in its history, after twelve days of talks. US inflation is down to 3.5 percent (February), and the rate banks charge each other is still near 8.75 percent.
why: Cheaper oil removes the last inflation scare that had lifted gold since the summer. From here gold drifts lower for two years.

title: The Fed raises rates for the first time in five years
what: On 4 February the Federal Reserve raised its target for the rate banks charge each other from 3 to 3.25 percent, its first increase since 1989. Long-term rates had come a long way down: the 10-year Treasury yield averaged 5.3 percent last October, against 15.3 percent in September 1981. Bond prices fell: the 30-year Treasury yield, 6.17 percent on 12 January, and the 10-year yield, which averaged 5.75 percent in January, are both rising. Inflation is only about 2.5 percent (January). The numbers: the Fed's rate 3.3 percent. Inflation 2.5 percent. Unemployment 6.6 percent.
why: The first shot of the 1994 bond massacre. Greenspan moved before inflation showed up, a pre-emptive strike that hurt bondholders badly in 1994 but set up the long boom of the late 1990s.

title: Sixth hike of the year as bond losses mount
what: On 15 November the Fed raised its rate target by three quarters of a point to 5.5 percent, its sixth increase this year, and banks raised the prime rate to 8.5 percent. The 30-year Treasury yield reached 8.16 percent on 4 November, up from 6.17 percent in January. Inflation is still under 3 percent, yet a 16-year zero-coupon Treasury has lost about 14 percent of its value this year. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.3 percent. Inflation 2.6 percent. Unemployment 5.8 percent.
why: The worst year for bonds in decades, with global losses later put at about 1.5 trillion dollars, and the backdrop to the Mexican peso crisis. Rates peaked in early 1995 and the bond rally that followed was enormous.

title: Britain will sell half its gold
what: On 7 May the British government said it would sell about 395 tonnes of gold, roughly half its reserves, in auctions from July; gold stood at 282.40 dollars that day. Gold averaged 276 dollars in May, its lowest monthly average since 1979. With inflation around 2 percent (April) and shares booming, few investors want a metal that pays nothing.
why: The emblem of gold's twenty-year bear market. The price bottomed at 252.80 dollars on 20 July, in the month the auctions began; 'Brown's bottom' became a byword for selling at the low.

title: Europe's central banks agree to limit gold sales, and gold jumps
what: On 26 September fifteen European central banks agreed in Washington to sell no more than about 400 tonnes of gold a year, 2,000 tonnes over five years, and not to expand their gold lending. The price jumped: gold averaged 311 dollars in October, 17 percent above September and up from a 20-year low of 252.80 dollars on 20 July.
why: The floor under gold's long decline. The price sagged once more in 2001, but the Washington Agreement marks the end of the bear market and the start of the long rise of the 2000s.

title: The Fed cuts by half a point, twice in one month
what: On 3 January, in an unscheduled move, the Fed cut its rate target by half a point to 6 percent, citing weakening sales and production, falling consumer confidence and high energy prices. At its meeting at the end of the month it cut by another half point, to 5.5 percent. As recently as May 2000 it had raised the rate to 6.5 percent to cool the boom. The surprise cut sent the Nasdaq up 14.17% that day, its biggest gain ever, and 12% over the month; beaten-down technology shares rebounded hardest, with Microsoft up about 41% in January and Apple 45%. The numbers: the Fed's rate 6.0 percent. Inflation 3.4 percent. Unemployment 3.9 percent.
why: The start of the 2001 easing: eleven cuts in one year took the rate to 1.75 percent, but could not stop the dot-com bust or the recession.

title: The Fed's rate falls to 1 percent
what: On 25 June the Fed cut its rate target by a quarter point to 1 percent, the lowest since the 1950s; since January 2001 it has cut thirteen times from 6.5 percent. Inflation is about 2.1 percent (May). The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 3.3 percent in June, the lowest since 1958, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 5.2 percent, the lowest since the mortgage company Freddie Mac began its weekly survey in 1971. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1.2 percent. Inflation 1.9 percent. Unemployment 6.1 percent.
why: Rock-bottom rates fuelled the housing boom that ended in 2008. Long bond yields bottomed in June 2003 and jumped by more than a point within weeks, a sharp loss for latecomers to the bond rally.

title: Greenspan's 'conundrum': long rates fall while the Fed raises
what: Since June 2004 the Fed has raised its rate target in quarter-point steps from 1 to 2.5 percent, yet long-term rates have fallen: the 10-year Treasury yield averaged about 4.2 percent in February against 4.7 percent last June. On 16 February Alan Greenspan told Congress that the behaviour of world bond markets 'remains a conundrum'. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.5 percent. Inflation 2.8 percent. Unemployment 5.3 percent.
why: Cheap long-term money, partly from Asian savings flowing into Treasuries, kept mortgage rates low and the housing bubble inflating even as the Fed tightened.

title: Seventeenth hike in a row; gold falls back from a 26-year high
what: On 29 June the Fed raised its rate target to 5.25 percent, its seventeenth quarter-point increase since June 2004, under Ben Bernanke, chairman since 1 February. Gold, which averaged 675 dollars in May, its highest since January 1980, fell back to an average of 596 dollars in June, 12 percent less. Inflation was 4.2 percent in May. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.0 percent. Inflation 4.0 percent. Unemployment 4.6 percent.
why: The end of the Greenspan-Bernanke tightening and a first test of gold's new bull market, which shrugged off the drop and passed 800 dollars within eighteen months.

title: Zero interest rates and the Fed starts buying bonds
what: On 16 December the Fed cut its rate target to a range of 0 to 0.25 percent, the lowest ever, and said rates would stay exceptionally low 'for some time'. In January 1981 the same rate had averaged 19 percent. On 25 November it had announced it would buy up to 500 billion dollars of mortgage bonds and 100 billion of mortgage-agency debt, and it is considering buying Treasury bonds as well. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 2.4 percent in December, and consumer prices in November were only 1.1 percent higher than a year earlier. Long Treasury bonds gained about a quarter in November and December. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.2 percent. Inflation 1.1 percent. Unemployment 6.8 percent.
why: The beginning of zero rates and quantitative easing, which lasted seven years and shaped every asset price until 2022. Long bonds gained while almost everything else fell.

title: Money is free: the Fed creates a trillion dollars to buy bonds
what: The Fed's interest rate has been at zero since December: banks can borrow almost for free. Because a rate cannot go much lower than zero, the Fed now uses another tool. On 18 March it said it would buy another 750 billion dollars of mortgage bonds and, for the first time, 300 billion dollars of government bonds, with money it creates itself. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.2 percent. Inflation 0.0 percent. Unemployment 8.3 percent.
why: The start of the age of free money. Buying bonds pushes long-term rates down too; the practice is called quantitative easing.

title: Two years at zero, and the Fed buys another 600 billion dollars of bonds
what: Money has been free for two years now, and the economy is still weak. On 3 November the Fed announced that it will buy another 600 billion dollars of government bonds, 75 billion a month, with newly created money. Its interest rate stays at zero. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.2 percent. Inflation 1.2 percent. Unemployment 9.4 percent.
why: The second round of bond buying ('QE2'). Critics warn of inflation; it does not come for another ten years.

title: The Fed promises: money stays free for two more years
what: Central banks rarely say what they will do far ahead. On 9 August the Fed did: it expects to keep its interest rate at 'exceptionally low levels', between 0 and 0.25 percent, 'at least through mid-2013'. Money has now been free for almost three years. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 3.6 percent. Unemployment 9.0 percent.
why: The promise is itself a tool: if everybody knows that rates stay at zero, long-term rates fall as well.

title: QE3: open-ended bond buying
what: On 13 September the Fed said it would buy 40 billion dollars of mortgage bonds a month, with no end date, until the job market improves, and that its rate would likely stay exceptionally low at least through mid-2015. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 1.5 percent in July, the lowest on record. Gold averaged 1,745 dollars in September, 7 percent more than in August. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 1.7 percent. Unemployment 8.1 percent.
why: 'QE infinity' marked the extreme of easy money; within a year the talk of ending it caused the taper tantrum.

title: Gold breaks down
what: Gold averaged 1,488 dollars in April, 7 percent below March and 16 percent below its peak month of September 2011. US inflation is only 1.5 percent (March), and shares are at records. The fear of inflation from the Fed's bond buying has not come true.
why: The start of gold's 2013 crash: the price fell 27 percent over the year and bottomed only at the end of 2015. A lesson that 'money printing' does not automatically mean higher gold.

title: Bernanke hints at slower bond buying and yields jump
what: On 19 June Fed chairman Ben Bernanke said the Fed could begin slowing its bond purchases, now 85 billion dollars a month, later this year. Shares fell about 4 percent in the next three trading days. Bond yields jumped: the 10-year Treasury averaged 2.3 percent in June, against 1.8 percent in April. Gold averaged 1,343 dollars, 5 percent less than in May. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 1.4 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: Just the hint of less support sent long rates up by a full point within months and hit emerging markets; it taught central banks to signal every step far in advance. Review 2026-10: 'taper tantrum' is the later label.

title: The Fed stops buying bonds, but money stays free
what: On 29 October the Fed ended its bond purchases. Since 2008 it has bought bonds worth about 4.5 trillion dollars with money it created. Its interest rate, however, stays where it has been for six years: at zero. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 1.7 percent. Unemployment 5.9 percent.
why: The end of quantitative easing in America; the first rate rise follows more than a year later.

title: Switzerland introduces negative interest rates
what: On 18 December the Swiss National Bank announced that from 22 January banks will pay 0.25 percent a year on large deposits held with it: a negative interest rate, meant to stop the franc from rising further. The European Central Bank began charging banks 0.1 percent on their deposits in June. In America the Fed's rate has stayed near zero since December 2008, and the 10-year Treasury yield averaged 2.2 percent in December, with inflation at 1.3 percent (November). The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 1.2 percent. Unemployment 5.8 percent.
why: The long fall in interest rates that began in 1981 goes below zero: savers pay to keep money at the bank, and safe government bonds are priced as if inflation were gone for good. The rates thread's low point in Europe; the US followed the same direction without going negative.

title: The first rate rise in nine years
what: On 16 December the Fed raised its rate target to a range of 0.25 to 0.5 percent, its first increase since 2006 and the end of seven years at zero. It said economic conditions would warrant 'only gradual increases'. Consumer prices were only 0.5 percent higher than a year earlier (November). Gold averaged 1,076 dollars in December, its lowest since 2009. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.2 percent. Inflation 0.4 percent. Unemployment 5.1 percent.
why: Lift-off ended the zero-rate era, and gold made its bottom the same month: the turn that started gold's next great rise.

title: Money stays almost free: the Fed holds its rate below half a percent
what: The Fed has kept its interest rate at 0.25 to 0.5 percent since December, after seven years at zero, and after Britain voted on 23 June to leave the European Union nobody expects it to raise the rate soon. Investors bought safe government bonds: lending to the American government for ten years now pays only 1.5 percent a year, less than ever before. Gold averaged 1,337 dollars, 5 percent more than in June. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.4 percent. Inflation 1.1 percent. Unemployment 4.9 percent.
why: The bottom of the 35-year bond bull market in its first form; yields only went lower in the 2020 pandemic panic, and the big reversal came in 2022.

title: A second small step: the Fed raises its rate to 0.5 to 0.75 percent
what: On 14 December the Fed raised its interest rate by a quarter of a point, to a range of 0.5 to 0.75 percent. It is only the second increase in ten years; the first was a year ago. Money is no longer free, but it is still cheaper than at any time before 2008. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.5 percent. Inflation 1.7 percent. Unemployment 4.7 percent.
why: The slow way out of zero: it takes three years to get back to 2.5 percent.

title: Three rises in one year: the Fed's rate reaches 1.25 to 1.5 percent
what: The Fed raised its interest rate three times this year, on 15 March, 14 June and 13 December, each time by a quarter of a point, to a range of 1.25 to 1.5 percent. Nine years after the financial crisis the economy no longer needs free money, it says. By the standards of the past, borrowing is still very cheap. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1.3 percent. Inflation 2.2 percent. Unemployment 4.2 percent.
why: Normalisation: unemployment is at a 17-year low, inflation near the 2 percent target.

title: The Fed cuts its rate for the first time since 2008
what: On 31 July the Fed lowered its interest rate by a quarter of a point, to a range of 2 to 2.25 percent. It is the first cut since December 2008, when the rate went to zero, and it comes after nine increases since 2015. The Fed speaks of insurance against a slowdown caused by trade disputes. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.4 percent. Inflation 1.7 percent. Unemployment 3.6 percent.
why: The way back to normal ends at 2.5 percent, half the level of 2007: the age of free money is not over.

title: Back to zero, and unlimited bond buying
what: As the coronavirus spread, the Fed cut its rate by half a point on 3 March and, on Sunday 15 March, to 0 to 0.25 percent, with at least 500 billion dollars of Treasury and 200 billion of mortgage-bond purchases. On 23 March it promised to buy bonds 'in the amounts needed' and, for the first time, to buy corporate bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 0.9 percent in March, a record low. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.7 percent. Inflation 2.3 percent. Unemployment 3.5 percent.
why: The biggest monetary rescue ever. The crash itself belongs to the pandemic arc; this beat explains why the recovery that followed was so fast and why inflation came back in 2021.

title: Gold at a record as the Fed says it will let inflation run
what: Gold averaged 1,969 dollars in August, beating its 2011 record. With the Fed's rate at zero, the 10-year Treasury yield averaged only 0.65 percent, below inflation of about 1 percent (July). On 27 August the Fed said it would now aim for inflation that 'averages 2 percent over time', allowing it to run 'moderately above 2 percent for some time' after periods below. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 1.0 percent. Unemployment 10.2 percent.
why: Negative real yields and a Fed openly tolerating inflation: the textbook case for gold. The new framework helps explain why the Fed was slow to react in 2021.

title: Inflation at 6.2 percent; the Fed starts to slow its bond buying
what: Consumer prices in October were 6.2 percent higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since 1990. On 3 November the Fed said it would begin reducing its monthly bond purchases by 15 billion dollars, while still describing inflation as 'largely reflecting factors that are expected to be transitory'. Its rate remains near zero. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.1 percent. Inflation 6.2 percent. Unemployment 4.5 percent.
why: The Fed was behind the curve: inflation reached 9.1 percent by June 2022, and the word 'transitory' became a byword for the error.

title: The Fed raises rates as inflation nears 8 percent and war breaks out
what: On 16 March the Fed raised its rate from near zero to 0.25 to 0.5 percent, its first increase since 2018, and signalled more to come; one member wanted a half-point move. Consumer prices in February were 7.9 percent higher than a year earlier, the most since January 1982. The Fed said Russia's invasion of Ukraine was likely to add to inflation. Gold averaged 1,948 dollars, close to its record. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.2 percent. Inflation 7.9 percent. Unemployment 3.9 percent.
why: The start of the fastest rate rises in forty years: the target reached 5.25 to 5.5 percent sixteen months later, and the 2040 Treasury lost about 30 percent in 2022, the worst calendar year for a bond in the game.

title: Inflation at 8.6 percent; a three-quarter-point hike
what: Consumer prices in May were 8.6 percent higher than a year earlier, the most since 1981. On 15 June the Fed raised its rate by three quarters of a point to 1.5 to 1.75 percent, its largest step in nearly three decades, and said it was 'strongly committed' to bringing inflation back to 2 percent; one member preferred half a point. A 30-year mortgage costs about 5.8 percent. The S&P 500 fell 8 percent in June to 3,785.38 and entered a bear market, down a fifth from its January record. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1.2 percent. Inflation 8.5 percent. Unemployment 3.6 percent.
why: The moment the Fed accepted it might cause a recession to stop inflation. Shares and bonds fell together, so a mixed portfolio offered no shelter.

title: Third giant hike; the British bond market breaks
what: On 21 September, with consumer prices still up 8.3 percent a year, the Fed raised its rate by three quarters of a point to 3 to 3.25 percent and said 'ongoing increases' would be appropriate. Britain's tax-cutting budget of 23 September sent British bond yields and the pound into a spiral, and on 28 September the Bank of England stepped in to buy bonds after pension funds came close to collapse. US 10-year yields neared 4 percent by month-end, the highest since 2008, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 6.7 percent. The S&P 500 had its worst day since 2020 on 13 September, lost 9 percent in the month and is a quarter below its January record. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.6 percent. Inflation 8.2 percent. Unemployment 3.6 percent.
why: The climax of the 2022 rate shock: bonds and shares fell together, and the gilt crisis showed how years of near-zero rates had left leverage hidden in 'safe' places. Review 2026-10: 'peak' was hindsight.
source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220921a.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_2022_United_Kingdom_mini-budget (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GS10 (read 2026-10-03); data/out/ust2030.json (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MORTGAGE30US (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20220921.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20221102.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_stock_market_decline (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, CPIAUCSL and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)

title: Silicon Valley Bank fails on its bond losses
what: On 8 March Silicon Valley Bank said it had sold over 21 billion dollars of bonds at a loss of 1.8 billion; customers withdrew 42 billion dollars the next day, and on 10 March regulators seized the bank, which had 209 billion dollars of assets. The bonds had lost value as interest rates rose. The authorities created a new lending facility for banks, and short-term Treasury yields fell sharply. On 22 March the Fed still raised its rate by a quarter point to 4.75 to 5 percent. Signature Bank failed two days later and regional bank shares fell sharply, but the S&P 500 ended March up 4 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 4.7 percent. Inflation 6.0 percent. Unemployment 3.6 percent.
why: The bill for the fastest hikes in forty years: bonds bought at near-zero yields sank, and a bank run followed. It marked the beginning of the end of the hiking cycle.

title: The Fed holds its rate at 5.3 percent, the highest in 22 years; mortgages near 8
what: The Fed has held its interest rate at 5.25 to 5.5 percent, the highest since 2001, since its increase in July; in early 2022 it was still zero. Long-term rates have followed: lending to the government for ten years pays 4.8 percent, the most since 2007 (in July 2020 it was just 0.6 percent), and a 30-year mortgage costs nearly 8 percent, the most in more than twenty years. Long-dated Treasury bonds have lost about 8 percent in September alone and are still falling. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.3 percent. Inflation 3.7 percent. Unemployment 3.7 percent.
why: The low point for bonds in the post-2020 cycle: from here yields fell sharply into December, and anyone who bought long bonds this month made double-digit gains within weeks. Review 2026-10: 'last' increase was hindsight.

title: The Fed's first cut in four years, half a point at once
what: On 18 September the Fed cut its rate by half a point to 4.75 to 5 percent, its first cut since 2020, saying it had 'greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent'; one member preferred a quarter point. Consumer prices in August were 2.5 percent higher than a year earlier, the lowest since early 2021. Gold averaged 2,571 dollars in September, a record, after central banks bought more than 1,000 tonnes in each of 2022 and 2023. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.1 percent. Inflation 2.6 percent. Unemployment 4.2 percent.
why: The end of the hiking cycle. Gold's new bull market, driven less by US interest rates than by central banks diversifying away from the dollar, had already begun.

title: Gold passes 4,000 dollars
what: Gold rose above 4,000 dollars an ounce for the first time in October and averaged 4,058 dollars, 11 percent more than in September. The Fed resumed cutting on 17 September and cut again on 29 October, to 3.75 to 4 percent, though inflation is still about 3 percent.
why: Gold's best year since 1979, more than 50 percent in 2025: rate cuts with inflation above target, central-bank buying and doubts about the Fed's independence.

title: Gold passes 5,000, then crashes on the new Fed chair
what: Gold rose above 5,000 dollars an ounce on 26 January and reached a record of about 5,600 on the 29th, as tensions over Venezuela, Iran and Greenland and fears for the Fed's independence drove buyers in. On 30 January the president named Kevin Warsh, seen as a defender of a strong dollar, as the next Fed chairman, and gold fell around 10 percent in a day while silver lost about 30 percent. Gold still averaged 4,753 dollars in January, 10 percent more than in December. The Fed has held its rate at 3.5 to 3.75 percent since December.
why: The blow-off top of the 2024-26 gold boom. The January peak was not regained by the autumn, and gold fell about 16 percent in the second quarter.

title: Inflation back above 4 percent; Warsh takes over; gold slides
what: Kevin Warsh, confirmed by the Senate 54 to 45 on 13 May and sworn in on 22 May, chaired his first Fed meeting in June, which kept the rate at 3.5 to 3.75 percent. Consumer prices in May were 4.2 percent higher than a year earlier, the most since 2023, after the war with Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz drove up oil prices this spring. Gold averaged 4,228 dollars in June, 8 percent less than in May and about a quarter below its January record. The numbers: the Fed's rate 3.6 percent. Inflation 4.2 percent. Unemployment 4.3 percent.
why: The oil shock turns the Fed from cutting to hiking. Gold, which had priced in easy money under a new chair, gave back much of its January surge as rate expectations rose; the causal link for the June slide is an interpretation, not a reported fact.

title: The Fed raises rates again as oil passes 100 dollars
what: On 16 September the Fed raised its rate by a quarter point to 3.75 to 4 percent, unanimously, its first increase since July 2023; the Committee pointed to persistent pressure in energy and consumer prices, and most members expect another increase this year. Consumer prices in August were 3.4 percent higher than a year earlier, and oil passed 100 dollars a barrel in early September as the conflict with Iran escalated. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged about 5 percent in September, the highest since 2007, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 7 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 3.8 percent. Inflation 3.4 percent. Unemployment 4.1 percent.
why: Where the game stands today: a second inflation wave in five years, and long bond yields back at levels last seen before the financial crisis.
